projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Paul Alexa was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II Veteran Paul Alexa. Mr. Alexa served with the U.S. Army 127th AAA Gun Battalion, Battery B. He served in Europe and his highest rank was PFC. I'm Tom Swope, and we recorded this at Mr. Alexa's home in Metro, Ohio, on July 1, 2001. Paul's age at the time was 84.

sp.speaker: Paul Alexa
sp.p: I was drafted in April of 1943, but in the latter part of 1942, I went into 1A. Before that I had been a supervisor in the machine shop during the war effort. And I went downtown, Clayborn, I thought, well, if I'm going to go I might as well go somewhere where I want to go, so I'd like to get in the Air Force. I went down to the recruiting station in downtown Cleveland, and the recruiting sergeant talked to me and after a bit he asked me, he said, How are you rated in the draft? What's your draft classification? I said, 1A. He said, Well, we can't take you. I said, What do you mean you can't take me? I want to go. I'm not going to wait until -- if I'm going to go, I might as well go now. I'd like to get in the Air Corps too.

No, he said, we can't take you. He says, The draft boards are complaining that we're taking too many 1As, and they can't fill their quota. So I said, Well, okay. So I went home and I had to wait until April when I finally got the call to go to the induction center. And I went there and I passed all the exams.

When I went through the line they asked me, You want the Army or the Navy? I said, You're not putting that monkey suit on me. I'm going in the Army. So I went into the Army, and I wound up in Camp Hon, California, an antiaircraft artillery camp. And there I was put into 120th antiaircraft artillery gun battalion. This was all new recruits, 17 or 18, 19 years old, but they called me Pop because I was 27 years old -- 26 or 27. And I was going through basic training there.

We had 90 millimeter guns, and I was on the range section. And my wife came out. And I was at Camp Irwin, which is now called Fort Irwin where the tank -- where they have tank maneuvers there. At that time it was just a desert camp. We had what we call a tent city. It was just nothing but parantal tents, and the whole battalion went out there. And the weather was atrocious, because it was about July.

And one day -- at that time I was an acting corporal. And they said, Who wants to go to electrical school for two weeks in Los Angeles? And with my wife in Riverside, California, I put my hand up. And they took me and sent me to Riverside. And from there I went to national schools in Los Angeles. Well, it turned out that after national schools in Los Angeles, about six or eight weeks, I went to Camp Davis, North Carolina, for further fire control work on fire control equipment. That was computers, director of the radar and the guns and all the equipment.

So I came back in November -- I got out in November. And at that time at -- I came out and I was awarded a ring because I had the best -- the highest grade in the class, both classes in Riverside, California and at Davis. And I got a 10-day delay en route. The guys were all waiting for 14 days delays en route, and I said I've only got a 10-day delay en route. And I was only one the papers that had a 10-day delay. And the ones that wanted 14 got 7 days.

But I had written a letter to the commanding general of Camp Hon, California, and I asked him -- I requested that I have a 10-day delay en route to visit my wife and family. Now, if he thought I had ten kids, why that's okay with me. So I got the 10-day delay en route. Anyway, after I got to California and I reported to Topside. There's a main camp and there was one that was an auxiliary camp I guess they called Topside. I went to Topside to report to the 120th. I was in B Battery, and here all these guys are all packing up and polishing their shoes. And I reported to the captain, and he said, We're going to go overseas tomorrow. And I said, Well, that's a heck of a note. I said, If I'd have known you were going to do this to me I'd never have left. Nobody likes to leave his outfit. Okay.

So I went back to the replacement depot, and I stayed there about a week and they took me out of the -- then they assigned me to the 127th AAA Gun Battalion, Battery B. Now, the 127th came from the 212th Post Artillery which was organized in 1918. And they made an antiaircraft outfit, because after World War I they wanted antiaircraft outfits. So they became antiaircraft. They had three-inch guns. And in 1940 they were activated, and they went to Camp Hood, Texas, I think it was, and they did some training there.

And then they set up their guns around Washington, D.C., and they set up and protected Washington for a while. And then they sent them to Seattle, Washington. And in Seattle, Washington, they again were protecting the aircraft plants and the shipyards in an antiaircraft row. And then the -- this was a 212th Regiment. The regiment at that time had maybe, oh, maybe 12 or 13 batteries. They had search lights, 37-millimeter guns, machine guns, and then they came out with the new radar, the 268 radar.

Then they came out with the new radar that I was on, I think it was 538. And SER5 Signal Corps Radio 538. And they broke up the regiment into battalions. And some of the battalions were made into 40-millimeter battalions which landed on D Day, and actually, on D Day were firing into the Germans right on the beaches with their 40-millimeter guns. The 90-millimeter guns didn't come in until a little bit later, because they were much heavier and more difficult to land.

Anyway, I got into B Battery, and here I find out that these guys were in the National Guard, with the National Guard Armory, and they had service stipes up to their shoulders. And all the rates were gone. All the jobs were gone. Here I came out of the Army, out of the school with this high grade. I thought that I should study because it's something that everybody would depend on me, I should know this stuff. And when I got out I thought they were going to make me a general, but I went in this old National Guard outfit.

They didn't even have a job for me, because at that time they only had one crew on each gun -- each gun had only one crew, the radar had one crew, the director had one crew. And so I was kind of like an extra man. I rolled cable and carried things around and that sort of thing, and I was kind of disgusted because I didn't have a job.

Well, when we got to England -- in July '44 we went to England. And at that time we didn't know that -- with our SER 568 radar, this was a gun lane radar, and it was so accurate. The most accurate piece of gun lane equipment that the Army had. We'd had an excellent record at Fort Bliss, Texas. We trained at Camp Hon, California, and then later on we went to Murrock Air Force Base and trained with the 4th Air Force. And today that's known as Edwards where they -- and at that time they had the first jet planes. And from there we went to Fort Bliss, Texas, which was an antiaircraft plant, and we trained there and in New Mexico. And from Fort Bliss, Texas, we went to Camp Shanks, New York, and then on a ship SYTHIA, the British ship SYTHIA.

We went to England, landed in Liverpool, and then we went to Blackshore Moors, picked up our equipment, cleaned up the cosmoline and everything on it, and then we went down to White Cliffs of Dover. We actually thought we were going into Patton's Army, but Eisenhower had loaned five American battalions -- five American battalions to the British to fight against the flying bomb.

Which at that time on June 11 I think the first ones came over, and they used to call the flying bomb the doddlebug and the buzz bomb. So sometime in July we landed on the White Cliffs of Dover, east of Dover Castle, and we set up our guns along east of Dover Castle. And our mission was to fire at the flying bomb.

Well, the first night that we were down there, it was raining. And we had set up our guns and the radar, and one of the things we had to do was start sandbagging and everything because of the shrapnel flying around. They didn't want to ruin this -- they didn't want our equipment ruined. We sandbagged the guns. Everything was sandbagged.

And once we got down to that first night, I was on a detail where we unloaded our trucks for our 90-millimeter ammunition. There were two rounds in a box weighing probably about 130, 140 pounds. And my buddies -- buddy Rosick and I were unloading these and putting them into a magazine. And it was a typical British night where it was raining, fog out on the cliff. And the sirens started up, air raid siren started up. And that was my first experience with an air raid siren, the eery sound of an air raid siren.

And I told Rosick, You know, Rosick, we better stay in the magazine, because somebody is going to get hurt around here. Well, we couldn't stay in there, we had to keep unloading the trucks. Anyway, we had -- we went on a 10-hour day. Ten on and ten off, so we needed two crews. So up until that time I had been on the -- I had been on the headquarter section, so my job was to work in the kitchen on KP, dig latrines, do guard duty, and any menial work that had to be done. But since I had gone to fire control school and had this good record, they needed a second crew. So I was put behind the radar, and I was very happy with that.

I went back on the radar. And since I didn't know too much about this particular radar, I got some books on it. And we started tracking the next day. And I was on the track when the first buzz bomb came over, and I got on it. And the radar tracks the bomb in horizontal range, that is the distance from the -- from us to the target. Then automatically the guns are -- the guns then raise themselves in elevation, and azimuth is the direction they turn around. And once you put the guns in -- once you get on the target -- you first picked up the target on a thing called a plan position indicator. And you can pick it up as a blip, a moving blip. And once you've studied the blip, then the plan position -- then the man on the range scope, on the scope itself, will crank out to the range that the plan on the plan position indicator tells you. Let's say it's 10,000 feet. You crank out to 10,000 feet, and what you will do is you'll pick up a circle and on it is an inverted U. It's a blip, and that blip is moving. So that tells you that's a moving target.

And you have -- you have a variable speed drive with two -- an inverted V again, I say a V, and you put the leading edge -- one edge of the V on the edge of this U, which is the blip which is the moving target. And you put it on there, and you adjust the speed so they're both moving at the same speed. Now you have the speed at which your target is traveling. And automatically in -- then in range, you're tracking him in range, then in elevation and azimuth, -- this is your target, your big dish will be turning around. You have a big dish with an antenna on it. And when everything is -- when everything is running smoothly, then the man on the range scope says, Put it in automatic. And up until that time you're tracking him manually. And the man on the plan position indicator hits the automatic button, and from then on all you have to do is just keep the speed right so that you keep the V on that inverted U as it moves around. This information is then sent to a computer.

That information you send to them is present data. Actually this is a trigometrical problem, because you have the range, which is the bottom of the leg, then you have the -- then you have the elevation, and then the height is computed because you have two legs of the triangle. And then, of course, all the time that you're turning around in azimuth you know the direction he's flying. Well, this data is then sent to the computer room. There's a computer, guy that's standing at a computer. And that is a present data. And with the speed of the -- known speed of the target and knowing how long it takes the shell, the antiaircraft shell to get up there and explode -- to get up there, because you cut the fuse, so many seconds. It travels at the rate of 2,700 feet per second. And then it calculates the future. And you shoot in the future. In other words, you're leading the target.

When all this data going in -- all this data is then transmitted to the four guns. When this data smooths out so that the guns aren't whipping around, the range officer will tell everybody -- tell the men to go into automatic, because at that time they -- there's an azimuth man and an elevation man, and they are tracking. All this information is coming to them as future information, and they're tracking it by hand. But when all this data smooths out so that the gun doesn't whip around and injure the men, because by that time the only man who has control of the gun is the man on the radar. And how smooth -- how well he does his job means how smoothly the operation will run and whether or not you'll shoot the target down. Well, then the range officer will then -- they're looking at a big you might say map of the area. And they are now tracking on this map, they are tracking the gun, the target. And they could tell when it comes at the most advantageous or closest range, when is the best time to start shooting.

Now, mostly we would shoot at no more than 5,000 yards. And then he would give the command to the gun sergeant to commence firing, and then the loaders would take the gun -- we had a proximity fuse which had a little radar in it, and it had a vial of acid in it. And as it went through the lands and groove of the guns, centrifugal force would break the vial of acid and it would start a little radar and it would start to put out a signal. It was proximity. When it got close to the target, it would explode. It was a very good device. The other way when we were using the mechanical fuse, the loader -- one of the loaders -- the gun would be sandbagged in a circle. And the shells were laid on the sandbags all the way in a circle so that the loaders just have to reach over, have a shell available. Well, the loader would pick it up and put it in the fuse setter. And the fuse setter would -- the fuse setter would then crank a handle, and he would crank the number of seconds that would be required for that shell to reach the target.

And then the -- one of the ammunition guys, he would put the shell on the breech of the gun. The loader would put it on the breech of the gun, and the gunner would be standing on the side, usually a corporal. And with the help of the loader, because sometimes you'd be at almost a 90-degree angle with a 65-inch shell, two men would have to push it up into the breech. And once it got into the breech and the breech block closed, he'd stand aside and pull the lanyard, and the gun would fire. The gun would eject the shell automatically in front of the fuse setter out to the front of the gunner, and the gunner would kick it out. Kick it out of the way.

Usually good gunners could kick it out over the guys' heads. Then another shell would be placed in there until the -- and they could fire as many as 30 rounds a minute. We had four guns shooting at a target, each battery. So there was a lot of ammunition expended. And then the command came to cease fire. Well, the first day I happened to be on the first shift, first bunch of guys that were -- first shift.

And when we got on the first bomb, I held on. I was able to hold on, and we shot the first flying bomb down. Later on when we got to Germany, one of my batteries shot the first airplane down. It was an ME109. A fighter plane. You had to be pretty good to hold onto that one. And one of the things we could track -- we could see the bursts in the scope as little asterisks. And you can also see the bomb explode in the air. Now, sometimes we knocked them down, sometimes we turned them around.

One morning about 5:00 in the morning I was on the radar tracking, and I was on the range scope. And one of the things, the commanding general come by and he inspected us. He said that he thought the men were sleepy at 5:00 in the morning, so we should drink a lot of tea laced with sugar. I thought that was a good idea, but I never got the tea. But anyway, this morning -- as I was saying, this morning I was -- about 5:00 in the morning, I was on the radar operating the radar, the range scope. And because we were shooting down so many of these flying bombs that the Germans started sending these flying bombs over in salvos together, because we could only get one at a time. I have to tell you that we were on the easterly portion of the White Cliffs of Dover, east of Dover Castle.

We were probably maybe about, oh, 5- or 6- or 700 feet off the edge -- from the edge of the cliff. And we used to -- in our time we used to go out, look at the channel as the Germans were shooting at the shipping going through the channel. And then the English would try to camouflage everything by putting the smoke screen down. And the ships would be in that smoke screen, but the Germans were playing cat and mouse anyway. You'd be shooting ahead of it or behind it. And we'd sit there watching this thing going on. Well, anyway, this morning that I was on the -- I was given -- always there was an early warning system, some very tall towers there. They went to a command center which was in the tunnels -- there were tunnels dug in the White Cliffs of Dover, right on the Dover Castle. And this command center would get the coordinates of a -- the flying bombs that come over or Nazi aircraft coming over, and they would then somehow or other transmit them to our positions.

And then our range officer would give the coordinates to those who were operating the radar. Well, I got the coordinates, and I had a headset on, phone on, and I got the coordinates and I would give them to the plan position indicator man. He'd get the coordinates, and then he would crank out those coordinates and see if they kept a moving target. And at that time we found out what the range was. This information ended up being transmitted to the computer. Well, this -- I got onto this flying bomb. One of the difficulties of the flying bomb was when you got an overhead -- when you got an overhead flight, of course the radar then when it starts changing direction and the dish would be moving so fast that you couldn't up and adjusting -- adjust the -- and hold the V on the blip, because it was moving, because it's a target. Of course, the target is moving.

As it come closer to it, the target would be moving faster. I don't know the distance of the target, the blip would go very slowly. Well, this one came over, and it came on an overhead course, but it must be a little bit away from us because I held onto them. And as it passes, we're firing at it, I can see the asterisk and the blips in the scope, and we miss him. Well, suddenly the speed of the target slowed down, finally came almost to a stop and started coming back. So that meant our range was coming -- our range was decreasing, that meant we had turned him around and he's coming back at us. So I was able to hold course, and I changed. And here I'm tracking him now and reducing the range, and we had missed him. And at that time the range officer came over, and he gave me a new set of coordinates. And I said, Sir, I think we've turned the target around because the range is decreasing. And he said, Yeah, I know, because he surmised that from being able to track it in the computer room, he says, But get on these new coordinates, which I did.

Well, as it turned out, our motor pool sergeant was on the road there going by. And in front of us -- back of us, there was a road. And he was going to one of the other batteries. And he saw what he thought was a fighter plane coming by. He said, Look at that crazy fighter plane, because it was coming towards us and had just missed the tall radar towers that are there in Dover. And after a bit he said, That ain't a fighter plane, that's a buzz bomb. Well, according to him, what they thought, he didn't know whether he should go backwards or forwards. Anyway, the bomb flew over, started heading low, just missed a hangar that C Battery just moved out of and exploded on the White Cliffs. Hit in front of us. So that was one of the dangers that we had. Another time I was pulling guard duty. And they put me -- my station was at the main gate coming into our camp. There was a road back there, and I had to guard that main gate. The British were on double British summertime, so they had daylight until about 11:00.

And so I may have been on from 10 to 11, 10 to 12 that day. And one of our guards was killed by the enemy shell fire from the night before, because it's 18 or 20 miles away on (Caproncher) Calais. The Germans had 15-inch guns, and they could fire one mile inland. And our ammo was sort of in an airplane hangar that was there from World War I. And Neismonger was guarding this ammo. And because a lot of it was just proximity to this ammo. And a fellow came to relieve him at midnight. And it was cold, so his relief wanted his overcoat. He asked Neismonger to go dry(?) it. And while Neismonger said, No, you know where it is, you get your own overcoat. While he was gone, Neismonger was killed. A shell hit him and blew him all apart. And that was the night before.

So when the Germans fired these guns, especially at night, there would be a flash. There would be -- you'd see these flashes of these guns on the French coast. And if you started counting, at about 80 they would hit. Now, I was watching the flashes as they were shelling the town of Dover, which was about four miles away. And I'm standing at my post and watching these flashes, and you could tell by the intensity of the flash if it was coming your way.

Well, suddenly the cloud -- the sky just lit up. They changed direction, and here are these very brilliant flashes. I said, Oh, hell -- you can say that. And the Navy and Army Air Force, similar to our PX, was staffed by some British civilians. And they served coffee and donuts, and there was a place where you could go to relax. And they had a sandbag dugout that they could go into when the shelling occurred. And they had benches along that dugout and a dim bulb.

And they had their World War I-type placoids on their head and sitting around there. I knew where it was, it was probably maybe l00 feet from where I was stationed on guard duty. And as soon as that happened, I ran for this dugout. I left my post. I ran for the dugout. And I got in that dugout, and the -- one of the nappy guys said, What's up, Yank? I said, Hold onto those pie plates. All hell is going to break loose outside at any moment.

Well, I had practically no sooner said that than the door opened and here comes through there Lieutenant McLean, my outfit. And he's officer of the day, and he's out checking the guards. We both looked at each other. The shells landed nearby, tremendous explosion, dirt and debris flying around. And he says to me, What are you doing here, Soldier? I said, Protecting myself, sir. I think I can do a better job alive than dead. And he said, I don't blame you after what happened last night. Return to your post. Well, I thought why is it that he can protect himself and I can't? So anyway I returned to my post and there was a dugout there, and I spent the rest of the time in that dugout.

Another time, we had kind of a serpentine trench around our area. And the orders were that when -- somebody was always watching -- say, One on the way, two on the way. And we're to dive into these trenches. Now, that didn't protect us from air bursts, but it did protect us from shrapnel flying around. But the Germans also had air bursts, and they'd fire these air bursts over our heads. If they couldn't get us with a direct hit, they'd get us from above. So one afternoon, since I was on a shift that -- I was on at night. I guess I was sleeping during the daytime. And it was in the afternoon, and they give us the warning that we're being shelled.

So it had rain that day, and it was wet in these trenches. So I was laying on my bed. I said, I'm just going to stay here. Now, the bed was a cot with my blanket on it. That was the mattress, blanket over me, but it was pretty good. So I ignored the warning to go in the trenches. And I'm sleeping there when the sergeant came in and said -- told me I should get my butt in a trench, which I did. When I came back, there was a hole through the roof, a piece of shrapnel was on the floor, and hole in my blanket. So I thought I was pretty lucky that I decided to go in there.

We did have passes, and one time I had a pass going into London. And one of the other types of -- besides the V1 bombs, the Germans had the V2, which was the rocket. There was virtually no defense for it, no defense. And I went into London on pass and went to the usual place, went to Westminster Abbey and places like that. Then at night I walked to Rainbow Corners or Salvation Army, so I was going to sleep at night. They had accommodations for soldiers that came in on pass. And they had a blackout. And, of course, it was black. I mean, I had a difficult time finding where I was going.

And I was asking, of course, pedestrians on the street, it was about 11:00, 12:00 at night, but there was traffic out too. Street traffic, especially the taxis. But finally I got into the hotel where I was at or Rainbow Corners, and I went to bed. And the warning came that we should get into a shelter. And I said, I'm sleeping between sheets, I'm just going to stay right here. Fortunately nothing happened. And another time Rosick and I decided -- whenever the shelling began, all traffic stopped. Nothing moved. Nothing moved in Dover anyplace. So there wasn't any shelling and we had some time off, so Rosick -- I told George Rosick, I said, Let's go into town and get a beer. So we walked the four miles into town.

We had to go down what they call Castle Hill into the main town of Dover, and there in Dover Square -- they had this square. And when we got there, there was shelling had commenced, and there was debris all over. There was debris all over. The only thing that was there was an American jeep was on the south side -- on the north side. We came in on the south side. On the north side was an American Jeep with some GIs in it. And we had to go to the toilet, and the pub that we wanted to go to was closed. And here we are with all this shelling going on, 15-inch shells dropping all over, so we decided we had better go to a shelter. So we went to a shelter, and it had a lot of people in it. And all we had to do was follow the directions of the signs. And we had a good time with the people. We shared with them what they had. Many of them were from London.

And one of them told me that they were from London, they were sleeping in the underground shelters. They're underground, and people would go there to sleep at night. And they said that they were going back to London. They came down here to get away from the V1s and the flying bombs and whatever they had in London. And they came back down there. And Dover was called Hell Fire Corner for the shelling that they endured since 1940. And it was a place where they thought the invasion would come in too because of the beaches, around Margate, Margate and Veal. The beaches were fairly accessible there, almost like in Normandy had big beaches. So well, then about midnight we had to be back on duty.

So about 10:30 Rosick and I left. We were still under shelling. And we were walking up Castle Hill, and it give us a pretty good view of the harbor and gave us a pretty good view of the guns. Fortunately, they were in a position where we could see the shelling. And we got back to our positions by diving -- ultimately diving into some trenches or behind a tree or wherever we could. Actually, you couldn't avoid a direct hit, but there was shelling. We got back to our camp all right. Well, about -- we had one incident where a shell landed in Dog Battery. It was in D Battery. We had Able -- I was in Baker Battery. Able, Baker, Dog -- Charlie, Dog. This was the Army alphabet.

It was about 11:00 one night -- one morning when we were shelling, and a shell landed in Dog Battery. And they had about 15-inch -- it was a humongous gun and they had about 15 casualties. They had about five men killed. And Gene Gerrecki, a buddy of mine, was on guard duty, was in his pup tent writing a letter to his parents. He was from California. And he was a Basque, and his father was a sheepherder. And Gene was writing this letter when a sergeant came by and said, Gene, go on guard duty. Well, Gene didn't tell him he had just gotten off guard duty, but he got up and took his gun and went on guard duty. And the shell hit near his pup tent, knocked it down, full of shell holes.

He considers himself a lucky PFC that he didn't complain about being on guard duty. And we had men there that was sitting on a latrine and had both their arms cut off, both their legs cut off right at the ankle. So it was a very dangerous place. I was orienting and synchronizing. This is where you -- the guns jump around quite a bit, so you have to get them oriented so that they are shooting at the place where the radar is telling them to shoot at. So when you orient and synchronize, you climb on top of the radar. And we have this big dish there, and there's a scope there.

And you pick a predetermined point in the sky, and you look through the scope. And the guns shoot at this predetermined point. There are tarolines in there, and they are calibrated from zero in the center out to about 5 or 10 mills to the left, to the right, up or down. And as the gun -- as each gun shoots, the observer on top -- which at this day was me. I'm looking in the scope, and I've got a headset on and microphone. And I'm telling the range officer where the bursts -- the position of the bursts in the scope so they can adjust the guns.

Well, I'm standing -- I'm up on top here looking. When the shell lands in front of the 3.7 millimeter British antiaircraft gun -- which they weren't using. They weren't as accurate as we were. It landed in front of them, but fortunately the shell landed in front of a concrete emplacement. It was a fixed gun, and the shrapnel went forward. And the concussion knocked me off the top of the radar. Fortunately I fell in a puddle of water. The only unfortunate thing was I had just --

I only had two pairs of fatigues, and I had just washed that pair. So I was stunned because it was a fall of about eight feet. And my buddy, Tom Eggers was yelling at me, Alexa, Alexa, how are you? Are you okay? I said, Yes, I'm okay. I said, Am I bleeding? He said, No. I said, Well, scratch me. I want to get a Purple Heart. Anyway, fortunately I came out of that just being stunned, but another 10 or 15 or 20 feet, it might have been a different story. And shortly after that, why we left.

The British took over, ran over the gun sites in the V1 positions, so we moved. And sometime in September I landed on Omaha Beach, which by that time was cleared of Germans. And I came -- I got there on a liberty ship in a convoy, and we came through this artificial harbor where they had taken a bunch of concrete platforms and old ships and taken the bottom off and made an artificial harbor, and we came inside the harbor. And after about four or five days -- three or four days, I forget how long it was, I climbed down the debarcation nets onto a rhino, which is a big barge up on the beach, and we got on our truck.

And then we spent a couple weeks around St. Margolais, which was the first town taken in Normandy until we got our assignment. And from there we went, and our first position was around Tongeren, Belgium. And Tongeren, Belgium, we didn't do any shooting at all because it was a little bit behind the lines, but then one of our positions was -- that was around Hocken, Germany. And we waited for the town that's called Gilinkershin -- we waited for the town of Gilenkershin to be cleared. And after it was cleared, we moved through the town and set up our guns in an apple orchard. And we were there at the apple orchard -- of course, we were outside the apple orchard. And we set up our guns there, and we did a lot of firing. Well, sometime later we moved from there.

One morning I was going to chow, which is -- they brought up a truck full of hot food. And -- yes, it was a morning. And as I was going walking along, I heard tremendous shooting behind me. And, of course, immediately I hit the dirt. And here a field artillery outfit had moved behind us, and they were shooting over my head. So I moved my pup tent up by the rest, and I moved my fox hole. I said to Rosick, We better get the heck out of here.

And one of the things that soldiers always look forward to is packages from home. So I came up with a unique idea of always knowing how many packages I was going to get. I told my mother and my mother-in-law and my wife, and I gave them numbers from 1 to 10, 11 to 20, and so on. I said you number your packages, and I'll always know when I'm going to get a package from home, because that was very important. Because I remember the first meal we had in Normandy after we'd been there about three or four weeks, we'd been on these rations, C-rations, which was a can of food, and a can of biscuits. And we'd been on that. It was either canned beans or canned hash or canned stew and some crackers and some pieces of candy, four cigarettes.

After you're on that for four or five weeks day in and day out, and for breakfast you had a K-ration. And we got tired of it. In fact, it was so bad you wouldn't have a bowel movement for a week. Naturally you wouldn't be eating much. Probably not a week, but it was a long time. Anyway, a truck pulled up and said, Hot chow. So I went up there, mess kits and I loved it ever since is oatmeal.

Somewhere they got some oatmeal and some powdered milk and sugar, and they were dishing this out. These guys were just hitting seconds and thirds. I went to an Army reunion sometime ago, I believe it was Kansas City maybe 10 years ago. And I asked one of our officers, I said, McCullough -- we didn't call him Lieutenant anymore. Say, Hey, McCullough, what was the first hot meal we had when we got to France? He said, Oatmeal. Nobody forgot it.

And we were in -- well, while we were in Gulinkershin, there were -- our dead people were -- our grave section came in and moved them right way. The only one that laid there for a couple of -- a day or two, I know, there was a colonel and his driver made a turn in the road and they hit a landmine. It killed them both. They were there for a day or so, but the Germans were on us, we buried them. Where there were foxholes, we buried them. We made a cross and buried them. Whatever happened to them later I don't know.

But Rosick and I went into town, the town of -- I said, Let's go into the town Louis. He said okay. So it was only a couple three miles away. The town was under artillery fire, but it was kind of sporadically. So he and I walked into town. We were going through the various buildings keeping whatever we could find, whatever we could carry, because the town was not occupied. Civilians had all left. I walked into a shoemakers shop, and he had all this machinery there and all his -- the floor was full of these wooden pegs. We looked around a little bit.

And as I walked through there, I walked between two greenhouses, and they had this plank between them. As we were walking behind us, here I hear this shell coming in. After you've been in shell fire, you know when a shell fire is coming into your back pocket because it has sort of a whir. You can hear the air going by. Maybe that's what causes the whistling of the shell, but I could hear the shell. So I lay down, glass and all. And that thing hit about 30, 40 feet from me, but it was a dud. Now, many of the -- I hear displaced persons worked on this, and they did something to the shells so there was a lot of duds.

So I told Rosick, I said, Rosick, the hell with Louis. We better get back to camp. We left there sometime later in, and we set up our guns in -- I kind of forget what was in between. But anyway, we set up our guns -- this was around the early part, maybe about the -- somewhere around when the Battle of the Bulge began. And we -- again, I was on guard duty late at night. And I played a lot of -- we played a lot of blackjack in between, because the radar in the wintertime was warm. We heated it with gasoline. So those of us who were off would sit around and play blackjack. So there was an awful lot of shelling going on that night.

I'm in my pup tent in the foxhole with Rosick. And we made it good and wide, because there was two of us would have to sleep in it. And I said, Rosick, let's go on the radar. I said, That's sandbagged. We'd sandbag a little bit. I said, I feel safer in the radar. It wouldn't have been if shrapnel would have come through there direct hit. Actually it was probably safer in the foxhole. So we went in there and started to play poker -- no, started to play blackjack. I was lucky. I don't know, I won about 50 or 60 bucks. I could hit a 14 with a 7 or 12 with a 9.

And as I went in there, I said, All hell is breaking loose out there. I said, I don't know what's going on but there sure is a hell of a lot of shelling. So we got orders at 4:00 in the morning, it was around 4:00, to pack up and leave. So we leave, and we were just about one step of the -- step ahead of the German Army, the tank corps anyways. I myself didn't know too much what was going on being in the range section. I knew what was going on in my little section; I didn't know anything about the General unless I read the Star and Strips. It was much later that I found out what the Bulge was. We didn't know the Bulge was a dent in the lines. We moved then back to another area where we did a lot of firing.

And then, of course, winter come in. It was very cold, below zero weather. And I remember that one day we would be moving every two or three days, getting new positions. And this one time we moved, it was around midnight, and the snow was a couple feet deep. We set up our guns, got them all oriented and synchronized. And I wasn't on duty, so Rosick and I set up our pup tent in the snow.

And we had learned that -- we had learned to acquisition -- requisition by theft a couple extra shell halves, and we made a mattress by getting some straw. We could always throw that in the back of our truck. And we kicked the snow aside and went to bed, went to sleep, and we sat in that position for two or three days. And there wasn't much activity with the Luftwaffe -- that's the German Air Force -- because the weather was so bad. So we set up in our position there, sat there for a few days.

And then on Christmas Day -- on Christmas Day it was a nice sunny day, and our American Air Force came out. And they were driving -- especially those guys in Bastogne, which we were maybe about five or ten miles from Bastogne. They were surrounded by Germans, and they were dropping supplies to them, our Air Force did. Then, of course, our fighter planes came out and there was quite a few battles going on. And, of course, then the paratroopers came in and they dropped in there. And eventually Patton come through, he broke through, and he liberated those people in Bastogne.

Well, during that period before they had -- well, the German offensive was to go onto the Muse River. They got within -- they got within several miles of it. In fact, I think one outfit really did get close to it, but the Muse River, if they got across it they could then circle around and go through Antwerp and surround a lot of American and British troops. And that way Hitler thought that they would win, because in 1940 he had broken through the Ardennes.

And our -- we were given a position in a small town, a village, which was a crossroads. And we pinpointed our guns on these crossroads -- the guns would be positioned because we were firing field artillery then. We could fire field artillery then too. And the captain called us together and he says, Well, you boys have been expended. We said, What do you mean expended? He said, We have to hold this position regardless of what. And I said, You know what, Rosick, turn your helmet around this way, they'll never which way we're going. I said, Turn your helmet around backwards. So we stayed there, and we did a lot of firing. And, of course, when you're on a range section you don't know what you're hitting, because you have forward observers and you're just relaying information to the guns. And the guns -- the gun sergeants and the range officer and the -- range officer and the gunnery officer, the gun officer, they're handling everything. So you really don't know.

I had to read off coordinates. It was coming off the phone to me and I would read off coordinates and they would adjust the guns and do the firing. And we also had what they called posit -- was it posit? We fixed up the guns and all of our equipment so we could blow it up if the Germans got close to us. It's not posit. I forget the name of it. But anyway -- thermites. Thermits.

And we had -- then after that I guess it's everybody for himself and get on a truck if you can. But fortunately, the actual push, the part of the Bulge that came close to us was about a mile and then the push was stopped. One of the things, the German Army didn't have enough fuel. And they wanted -- what they had to do was get within -- kind of use captured fuel. If they captured trucks, they took the gas cans off the trucks and filled their tanks up. And they had a big tank.

One of the other things was that the German tiger tank was so big, or panther was so big that the roads in Belgium weren't up to date, and they were having a hell of a time moving along. But had they come along with -- the name of the guy was Colonel Piper, German Piper. They went to one place and they made the wrong turn. Had they turned left instead of right they'd have come to Laglase and come to a huge American gasoline dump, and they would have had all the gasoline they wanted. And if they would have got that, they could have captured the only bridge they could have used. They could have captured that bridge, and that was at Laglase. And so at Laglase, they were ready to dump all that ammo and burn it.

And I guess in the heat of Battle of the Bulge, why they did burn -- some of them they did burn their ammo so they wouldn't get it. And so we stayed there in that position, then we moved back. And we moved back around Liege, and we gave antiaircraft protection to Liege.

On New Year's Day, it was a nice, bright sunny day, and the Luftwaffe came out. And, of course, the flying bombs were coming over all the time. And the Luftwaffe came out, and by that time they had fighter planes. They switched to fighter production rather than bombers to try to beat the American -- to beat the Air Force, British Air Force, they'd shoot them down. Anyway, I was going to chow early in the morning, and we had a -- there was an orchard, and there was a metal -- a wooden building in there. And so our range station, we moved into the wooden building. And we knocked part of the building off and made bunks, and we slept in the bunks.

Anyway, when these two German fighter planes came by and strafed our area. Then some flying bombs came over, and I was going to chow, and I heard this flying bomb come over -- that was in the evening when I saw this flying bomb come over. It had a light on the back. You could see the light, the exhaust was a bead of light, so you could follow this light. So I heard this flying bomb coming over and I'm watching it. And I stood there watching it, and it seemed that everything that you yourself would change position it would change position too and follow you.

And it would pass over my head, and then all of a sudden the engine cut out. And when it cut out, there was this screaming sound. They equipped it with wires or whatever they did, it came with a screaming sound. Well, I hit the dirt. And mess kits and all flying, I hit the dirt. I don't remember if there was snow or not. And I know that I lay down. And the bomb hit, oh, I'd say maybe 500 feet from me. A distance away, it was -- which with, probably with the speed of the bomb was probably half a second or a second was all after it flew over my head.

And it hit close to our -- close to our mess truck. Trucks were -- food was always served on a mess truck, and a mess truck would come up. And fortunately it missed the truck. They had a fly set up so you could just get your food under the fly. And I guess it knocked the fly down. So I went there and I looked at this hole, you could put my house into that hole. And one day while we were there, one evening, a buddy of mine by the name of Ryan, there was a little town in back of us. I don't know what the name of the town was, there was a restaurant and a tavern.

So he came to me and he said, Let's go back there and get ourself a drink. We can probably get some schnapps or cognac or something like that. I said, Okay, Ryan. Good Irishman, you know, he wanted a drink. So we went back in there. It was night. And it seemed like it was the end of buzz bomb alley because the buzz bombs were always landing in there. And I told Ryan, I said, Ryan, we're going to get killed back in there. No, he said, they couldn't hit a bull with a bass fiddle. I said, Okay. So we went there. And we were sitting in the kitchen, not in the bar. I'm telling you some of the things we did off duty too, you know. We snuck out a little bit. And we're in there. We're drinking this cognac. And we're sitting there drinking this cognac, and I said to Ryan, I said, Hey, Ryan, this thing sounds like it's got gasoline in it.

Nah, it don't. It sure does. Taste it. So he's drinking it. And after a while the proprieter went into the bar, which was a long bar. And he got a jug out and he starts filling that jug up. Then he got a tin can out with that conical-shaped top and unscrewed the top, and he looked at me and he said, Benzene. I went back and I said, Ryan, don't light that cigarette. Holy crap, you'll blow up. So we went back in there. Another time we were off duty. And Ryan was a gunner. He's a guy that shoved -- he was a big guy. He shoved the shell into the gun.

And when we were in Normandy, I had acquired a bottle of Calvados, which they called white lightening, which was made of apple juice, apples. There were a lot of apple orchards in Normandy. And this was around Christmastime. So we were sitting around in this wooden building that we had made, and we'd commandeered a stove someplace. Whenever we wanted something, we would call on the German people and we would commandeer a radio, a wood stove, or whatever. And we would make out a receipt for it. And we'd say this was for the American Army and we would sign it. We'd ask the name of it, and if it had a serial number, we'd put the serial number. And then we would sign it Sergeant Joe Palooka.

Anyway, we had some drinks, and he said, I know a restaurant in town. It was really dark, and it was dangerous because there were Germans in American Army uniforms that were dropping in that area, because this was during the Bulge. And I said -- so we walked into this town not too far away from our position. It was snowing that night. And we went into this restaurant, and one thing I remember about it, we had some cognac. And I remember a woman had a turkey, and she gave me a turkey leg. And that was something, to eat a turkey leg.

So Ryan got pretty well bombed in there. I said, Ryan, we got to get you back on duty, because he was going on duty. The guns worked a little different than we did on the radar. I said, I got to get you back on duty. So we left town. We walked into town. And somehow or other it was dark and snowing. I found my way out of town when suddenly we were halted. We were stopped, and here was American troops stopped us. And they started questioning us. And they took us to a CP. There an officer questioned us. He said, What are you doing? I told him, I said, We just went in to get a few drinks. He asked me a few questions. He says, Where are you at? I said, We're with the AA outfit up the road. He said, Don't you guys know any better? He said that there's Germans in uniform out there that were killing people, he said, in American uniforms.

You should get back to your outfit right away before somebody kills you. So while at the restaurant, a woman gave me a 25-year-old bottle of raisin brandy. And I had a couple schnapps, a couple sips of it, and it was good stuff. 25 years old, she told me. This was a Belgium woman. We got back there. I got Ryan back to his gun. And his gun commander was named Tiny. And Tiny was a great big guy. And Tiny looked at him -- we might have been a few minutes late. I explained to him what happened. I said, He's okay. Nothing happened to him. I got back. The next day I went back, I said, I left that raisin brandy, I left it over on the gun pit. I went back there but I was too late, see.

So those were some of the things that we -- whenever we could, we'd visit with some of the locals. And we traded all the time. We would trade cigarettes and chocolate for apples, maybe homemade bread, and that sort of thing. Well, then after the Battle of the Bulge, I made the Rhine River crossing at a town called Julich, J-u-l-i-c-h. And from there we went towards Cologne. And I said to him -- I said to myself, if I was going to rebuild a town, I'd never rebuild Julich. It was just rubble. And the engineer said we could cross the river, and we crossed it on a rubber pontoon bridge. And I never liked those damn things, because we were going across on a six by six and you're bouncing up and down. It was in the wintertime, and I could see what would happen if I ever fell in that water.

Fortunately we got across okay. We went through Julich, and then we moved up changing positions until we got to Cologne, shooting along the way doing various things. I really didn't know what we were doing. We'd move into a position and we would shoot -- we'd shoot antiaircraft. And I'd go on the -- do my job on the radar. Although I do have every letter I ever wrote to my wife, although -- probably I'm going to have to go through them, because some of them I may have mentioned something, but they were always -- they were read by an officer. One time he took the word "convoy" out.

After I got to England, I wrote that we had come through on a convoy. He took "convoy" out. What the hell are the Germans going to do with a word like "convoy"? Anyway, so when we got to Cologne and we stopped at a town called Minchengladbach or Monchengladbach. And we stopped at Monchengladbach, and we were at Monchengladbach and set up our guns there. And the roads were just full of artillery antitank guns, our tanks, infantry, of course all moving up ready for the crossing of the Rhine River. And we got orders to go to Wesel. And there General Montgomery took over the -- we went out of the 9th Army and we went -- I guess the 9th Army was put under Wesel -- under General Montgomery, and he handled that, that crossing. And we were about -- fairly close to the Rhine River. I couldn't see it, but maybe half a mile from the Rhine River. And they were putting up a railroad trestle.

So we guarded that railroad trestle so that they -- the Germans couldn't knock it down. Every day we were getting ready to get what they called Bed Check Charlie would come over and we'd be shooting at him, you know, and never did hit him. Well, he was flying low, you know. And one of our gunners -- this was during the Bulge -- the day that we were being strafed, why again we were being strafed.

And one of our machine gunners, Joe Dankle -- we had quadruple-mounted machine guns too, 450 calipers, one guy sitting in the middle shooting at it. And he shot down an ME109, German, and shot it out of the sky. That same day we shot down an American P47, because apparently he had been over the line, he got shot up, so he was limping back. And he came in during the time when the FW09, which was a regular engine plane, and so was the B47s was a regular engine plane, only it's pear shaped. It wasn't perfectly round.

We should have known the difference. But in the heat of battle, we said, Here comes another SOB, and we opened up fire at him, small arms and all. Well, they crippled him up bad enough they picked him up. He was able to get out of the plane and brought him back. He was a little upset. But Dankle, the next day our colonel, Colonel Jacob Reynolds, and he said -- he used to tell his men, I want to be called Iron Jaw. He wanted to be called Iron Jaw. And we had another name for him. Anyway, Reynolds come over, and he wanted to congratulate the machine gunner. And he got to Dankle and he asked Dankle about it. We asked Dankle, Hey, Dankle, did you see all the -- when you were shooting at this guy, didn't you see all the dust flying around you?

Yes, I was shooting at him too, see. And he said, No. And the colonel said that -- interviewed him, said to Dankle, How old are you? Dankle said, 19, sir. He said, I'm going to give you a bottle of whiskey, but Army regulations say I can't give you a bottle of whiskey, he says, but here's a cigar instead. So he gave him a cigar.

And a number of years ago I visited Dankle in Philadelphia, maybe 10, 15 years ago. He came to visit me. I visit -- we came from -- off of 41 states, so I got buddies all over the United States I visit. Anyway, I visited him. We were having dinner, and I told the story, and they never knew about it. Never knew that Dankle got a cigar for shooting that plane down. He told me, he said, Well, I'm 19 years old. He said, I'm old enough to shoot airplanes down but I can't drink.

Then we were at Monchengladbach, and we sat around in there. One of the things the Germans were doing, they were floating mines down the Rhine River so that they would try to blow up these bridges. And then they put a pontoon bridge all the way across. Pontoons are nothing but these great big rubber life rafts, you know. Single lane, and the tanks and everything would go across. That's how I got across. And I don't know if it was C or D Battery were the first ones to go across. And they probably got across on the second day after the bridge was done, which the engineers put it up in a hurry. And they set up -- these guys set up on the bank and were shooting at whatever floated down the river.

And Bob Miller, a buddy of mine from C Battery, was sleeping on the bank. And he was shooting -- one of those guys shooting, but he had his pup tent set up there. And sleeping in a pup tent. He changed positions one night. Where he had his head he put his feet, and he got shot in the feet that night, the legs. And I saw him and I said, Hey, Miller, you horse's behind, and you got yourself a million dollar wound. You're going back to the States.

He did, they sent him back to the States. But this is one of the things you had to worry about, because, you know, he might have got shot by one you us or he might have got shot by the -- probably might have been one of ours, I don't know. But anyway, so there was quite a bit of shooting there. And it was during that time that we heard that Roosevelt had died. And then --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was the reaction when you heard about Roosevelt?

sp.speaker: Paul Alexa
sp.p: In Wesel, Wesel, Germany.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was the reaction of the men?

sp.speaker: Paul Alexa
sp.p: I didn't have any real particular feeling. I felt bad that he died, but nothing real bad, you know. Roosevelt was a president, he was my president. I felt sorry for him that he died, but his picture was in the paper, you know, at these various meetings where they showed a man who was sick. So then Harry Truman, I didn't feel anything bad about Harry, because Harry was a captain in World War I. In fact, I like Harry particularly that he ended the war, because Harry knew the casualties that we were going to assume, because after the war was over, we started to train -- I was on a detail moving our equipment down to the Marseille where we were going to go to the Pacific. And two batteries were doing that and two batteries were training -- going into training for Pacific-type warfare. And I was in Metz, France, when I heard that the buzz bomb had been dropped -- not the buzz bomb, but the atom bomb had been dropped. And I always felt real good about Harry, because I didn't know what would happen when I was going over there because, you know, my cousin was on a ship about ready to go through the canal. And he started in Africa, and he was going to go through the canal when the atom bomb dropped and they diverted him off to New York. But then we made the Rhine River crossing, and we again set up our guns and protected that bridge until they completed the railroad bridge and gave aircraft shooting at --antiaircraft protection. And then we got our orders to move up. And we started moving up, maybe a day at a time digging in, always digging in, moving, digging in. And we finally stopped about 65 miles from the Elbe River where we met the Germans. And then we went into -- immediately we went into rounding up German prisoners of war, guarding this displaced persons camps, guarding prisoner of war camps. At first they didn't have a camp. They would just have a big circle of wire and put the German prisoners inside of the wire. And the orders were anybody tries to escape, goes beyond the wire, shoot them. Well, I never shot them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did some try to escape though?

sp.speaker: Paul Alexa
sp.p: Did they try to escape? Yes. I think some of them just wanted to commit suicide, because I don't know how they fed all these guys. It must have been a terrific logistical problem. Then later on it became more organized, and they had them in camps, former camps that the American prisoners were in, especially the aircrafters. And they had the SS prisoners, which were the elite German troops, and we had them in camps and I guarded them. And we had camps where we had displaced persons, and they lived in the camps. And we had to guard the camps to keep them in there because they wanted to go and kill all the Germans they could, especially if they lived in an area where they lived on a farm and they were mistreated. They would go out and kill the people, kill the farmers in the house and burn the farm down. I remember one farmer came up to us, I was in -- I was in a -- had of logger where we had about 2,000 displaced persons I was guarding. 16 or 18 of us were guarding them. And we -- you know, there would be a square enclosure. We'd put a guard on one corner, one guard in the opposite corner. You know, one would be in the northwest corner and another one would be on the southeast corner. And anybody jumping the fence would got shot at. Well, I said, just shoot over their heeds. And there was a main gate, and sometimes we would be at the main gate. These guys always wanted to come out. They said -- the displaced person wanted to go see someone. They weren't armed in the daytime, we would let them out. We couldn't hold them all in there. Keep them all in. And they always wanted to go see the schneider, that's the tailor, or to get some holtz. The good things about it is that it was close to a town called Steinhagen. And Steinhagen had a distillery there, and they made Steinhagen, which is a good German whiskey. Have you ever heard of Steinhagen? Well, Steinhagen was a German gin. And it is good. Every time I go into a German restaurant I ask them if they have any Steinhagen, and I get myself a Steinhagen martini. And I'd be on the main gate. They'd be asking me, Vodo? Vodo, why can't we go out? I said, Because the commandant says so. That's why you can't go out, the commandant says so. But, I said, I tell you what, you bring me a bottle of Steinhagen, and you can go out. So I get off guard duty, and we had a fire house that we'd stay in. We'd have some Steinhagen. And Joe Miller was a warrant officer, and he was in charge of our group. We had a small group, 16, 18 men around guarding prisoners in camps all over, see. Out of 700-some men, we did a lot of duty like that. And Joe Miller come by in a Jeep one day, and it was daylight. Wanted to inspect us. And I was at the camp. And one guy was just asking me how come he couldn't go, and I told him about the commandant. I says, Here comes the commandant now. So the commandant came in there, and this guy looked at him and says, Commandant, pzzzzzz. Gave him the raspberries. Well, another time we're in another area, and I had a little more time at night. A German farmer came and asked me to get some guys to go sleep at his house at night because these displaced persons were coming in and raiding and killing people. And he said would we come and spend the night in his house and chase these people away. So I talked to a couple of buddies of mine and said sure. I said, Hey, we'll get to sleep in a (inaudible) tonight. So we went there -- went to his house, fed us a big meal. And then after dinner they had some good double cognac, good schnapps. And we had cigars. We would give them, good cigars. The old man there was a grandfather. I guess he was the patriarch of the family. I gave him the tube of cigars. He was puffing on the cigars. You could see how much he enjoyed them. Well, we went to bed. And the men would stay up all night. They had a long brass horn, something like these horns they blow at the race tracks. And when he'd blow on the horn, that means that the Russians are coming, the displaced persons are coming. Then at that time we would get up and chase them away. And, of course, how often they would come back I don't know, but they come back a couple times. But that was pretty good duty because then we got a good meal. Then we'd come back at night. And anyway, after we made the Rhine River crossing, why then the Americans met the -- met them at -- the Russians at the Elbe River. And there were other incidents that would probably come to my mind, but that's kind of an overall view of what my outfit did. Everyday shooting, one time we shot 700 antitank rounds. You'd hit these tanks. One of the things about a tank when you hit it, it burned up because you hit the fuel. And the guys loved to shoot. And the flying bombs, curiously we couldn't shoot at flying bombs once we got on the continent, and there were a lot of them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: A lot of them by then?

sp.speaker: Paul Alexa
sp.p: There were many coming over, but we couldn't shoot at them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Because they didn't want them to fall?

sp.speaker: Paul Alexa
sp.p: I don't know what the reason was. They wanted us -- well, at one time we were limited to four rounds of ammunition per gun to shoot. I guess bringing all the ammo and the ammunition up, you know, because what they do, they used to bring up all the supplies and park it alongside the roads and the trucks used to go by and pick it up. I guess maybe that was it. And they felt that the V1s were going -- some outfits shot at them. I know those at Antwerp, they were headed to Antwerp where they had a big gun belt around Antwerp. In the Mostrick area, in the St. Pierre Mountains, there are some caves in there which were supposedly started by the Romans.

And these caves are quite extensive and deep. And these caves have been used for protection for years. And the walls are just covered with drawings. It's a marl-type of -- whatever marl is, type of construction, cave drawings, sculptors. And they're very deep. In fact, a Dutch citizen took me and Rosick through there when we were in the Mostrick area, because I had befriended him. He was an electrician in a camp that made -- factory that made cement. And I had given him some food and things for his kids. So one Sunday, why he came over and we got off duty and we made this trip. And he had a flashlight. He showed us the inside of these caves. And in these caves are many, many drawings, go back hundreds of years.

And in fact, the smudges up on the ceiling that when they were first mining this sandstone, they had smudge pots to light, and the soot is still on the ceiling for hundreds of years. Anyway, on Christmas -- Mostrick was liberated about September. And on December 24 of 1944, somebody came up with the idea to hold mass for the American troops in this cave. And so the announcement was made that if you want to go to mass on December 24, so we got up on trucks and they took us to the caves, got lost along the way. Took us into the caves. And an alter had been set up, a space had been prepared on the wall, flat on the wall. And on it there was a saying that these Brothers of the Immaculate Conception wished that we would get home early, so on and so forth.

Father Brazinski, an American chaplain, had the mass. He was later killed in action. And the brothers who run the cave, Catholic brothers, had a choir. They ran the cave. And the cave had about 300 or 400 GIs in it. And mass was held, confession before mass, very rapid. And some of the monks came in on Jeep also. They were transported in on a Jeep. And they didn't know what was going on, because when they saw these American troops in there just out of the fields, unshaven, with their soiled uniforms, rifles on their back, and just brought in from a combat zone. And after the mass was over, there were photographs -- many photographs were taken.

And after the mass was over, why on the prepared space on the wall with charcoal of some sort everybody wrote his name on the wall. In fact, we couldn't even get the whole -- everybody signed before the orders came to load back up on the trucks and return to combat. And the next morning about 800 men left that area for the Battle of the Bulge, and about 50 survived.

And most of them are now buried at the Margot Cemetery in nearby Mostrick. So now since that time beginning about 1980, Charles Smithoyzen, who was a Dutch partisan, came up with the idea of having a memorial mass commemorating that mass. And they have mass there every year since 1980. And Allen Engrishin from our group is the only one that's ever been back to the mass. I was supposed to go with him, but something turned up and I didn't go. And he has been back there. And now there is a group of people who commemorate that who have formed an association.

And, of course, they want to find out how many men are available that could go to that mass, so if only 50 are available I don't know how many are alive, but that mass is held every year. And this year, why the good Lord willing, Ellen and I said we would go to the mass on Christmas Eve. Anyway, finally the day came I got on a ship.

And after a 17-day crossing, why I landed in New York State. One day -- they would post on a board how many miles we had traveled every day. One day because of inclement weather we went 75 miles in a 24-hour period. And we spent our time playing cards. I played poker most of the way. And I won about $2,000, which made a nice down payment on a home when I got back. And that's how we spent our time. I've got photographs of us on the ship. And the weather was so rough -- this was a liberty ship. And they also assured us that it wouldn't break in half, because it usually would break in half between the second and third holds or fourth holds, that they had welded an extra strip all the way around.

I went on there and took a look at it to see was it there. Yes, it was there. Extra with the metal so it could hold it together. It was so rough the ship pitched. One day I was standing near our hold going down, and the ship pitched and you could actually see the prop come out of the water. The guys would holler, This is no airplane. Put that back in the water. And we landed in New York City, and we went to -- I think it was Camp Roberts and got off the ship.

I saw the Statute of Liberty for the first time. Came down off the ship, and the first thing we got was a carton of milk. Our first milk from the time we left the states. And then we got on a train, and we got to camp. And after we got settled in there a little bit, they took us to mess hall and gave us a big steak dinner. The captain who was in charge gave us a speech and told us that -- wished us well in our civilian life and that -- and he told us about the things that we had gone through during that time in the Army, especially overseas.

And I finally got to telephone, I called my wife. Well, she had been following -- I came home with the 110th Infantry Division and what company I was. She had -- the paper used to publish who was coming in the states, so she was following it. And finally she saw that the 110th Infantry Division came in. And she had been following us. So when I first called, when I had a chance I called her, and, of course, she was thrilled, and I was thrilled to see her. And I told her, I said -- I said at that time I didn't know when I was going to come home. It all depends on the separation center.

And at the time that I got blown off the radar, I had injured my back, so I was going to medics about it. And they wanted to send me to a hospital. I said, No, no, you're not sending me to the hospital, because if they go to the hospital, you don't come back to your same outfit. I was thinking on the front line someplace, and I said knew that. And I said, No, no, I'm going to come back with my outfit. Everybody -- they didn't want to leave their outfit. So on my records they had put -- they had that -- they had put something in there about the injured back. And I think it was ailing back, which is different from what it was -- maybe it was ailing, injured, ailing, something like that.

So then I went through -- I give a guy 20 bucks, which I still have today, for his money belt so I could put my money in a money belt. And then I called my wife, and then I went -- from Camp Roberts I went to -- I went to Indiantown Gap near Philadelphia. And I spent a couple days in Indiantown Gap and got my discharge papers. Well, before you get -- before you get discharged, they interview you, ask you all about have you got anything hurt or anything like that. The officer asked me about my back. I told him what had happened. I don't know if this guy was an officer, I guess he was. And he said, Well, we'll keep you here for a while. We'll examine you. I said, Well, how long are you going to keep me here? He said, About a week.

I said, No, I'm going home. I'm married. I said, I got a wife waiting for me at home. I should have gone, because I still have pains today. But anyway, because the guys who were on the guns are hard of hearing. They're all getting pensions. I could see why they'd be hard of hearing with that damn gun cracking all the time, you know. So my wife met me alone. She said, I didn't want any of the family there when you came home, which I wouldn't liked anybody but her too, you know.

And she met me at old Pennsylvania Railroad Station at East 55th Street. And we got a taxi and came home. And she had big signs all over, Welcome home. We lived upstairs in a double house. And I was very happy to come home. And couple of nights after I was home, I got up during the middle of the night like this and at that time there weren't any interstates. And the big trucks used to go up and down roads with their noise, you know. And I heard this thing, and I looked up and I said, Buzz bomb. My wife said, What? After a while it just dawned on me, I came to, Oh, nothing. I said, Nothing.
(End of interview)
